title: Compliance for regulated industries: what changes when rules apply
hook: Finance, health and other regulated areas add hard requirements, like explainability, audit trails and approvals, that a general-purpose assistant doesn't need by default.
inPlainWords: When an AI feature touches a regulated area like payments or health data, requirements such as record-keeping, human sign-off and explainability stop being optional and start being things you must prove, not just claim.

useCase.title: The assistant now helps with payment disputes, not just returns
useCase.story: ShopEase is adding an assistant feature for payment and chargeback disputes, which touches financial regulation. What was optional for general support, like explanations, audit logs and human sign-off, becomes required, and the team must show evidence, not just claim compliance.

approaches.name: Treat it like any other assistant feature
approaches.what: Ship with the same guardrails as the general support bot.
approaches.avoidWhen: Always avoid this once financial, health or similarly regulated data or decisions are involved.
approaches.example: Shipping a payment-dispute feature with no audit log, discovered only during a regulator's request.

approaches.name: Map which specific rules apply before building
approaches.what: Identify the actual regulations and requirements that apply to this specific feature and region, not a general sense of "compliance."
approaches.avoidWhen: Never skip; building first and mapping rules after means expensive rework.
approaches.example: Identifying which disclosure and record-keeping rules apply to payment dispute handling in each region ShopEase operates.

approaches.name: Add an audit trail for every decision
approaches.what: Log what data was used, what the model output, and what the final decision was, retained for the required period.
approaches.example: Every dispute decision logs the input, the model's reasoning summary, and who approved it.

approaches.name: Require human sign-off above a threshold
approaches.what: Automate routine cases, but require a qualified person to approve anything above a defined risk or value threshold.
approaches.greatWhen: Regulations require accountability to a specific person, or errors carry real financial or legal cost.
approaches.avoidWhen: The threshold is set so low it defeats automation, or so high that risky cases slip through.
approaches.example: Disputes under $50 auto-resolve; anything above requires a named reviewer's approval.

approaches.name: Build in explainability, not just an answer
approaches.what: The system must be able to state which facts and rules led to a decision, not just produce one.
approaches.greatWhen: Regulations or customers have a right to an explanation.
approaches.avoidWhen: Never skip where such a right exists.
approaches.example: A denied dispute cites the specific policy clause and transaction detail that led to the decision.

challenge.question: The team is extending the assistant to payment disputes, a regulated area. What should happen before writing any code?

options.text: Map the specific rules that apply to payment dispute handling in each region, then design audit trails, sign-off thresholds and explainability around them
options.why: Regulated features have concrete, specific requirements; discovering them after building risks expensive rework or real violations.

options.text: Ship using the same guardrails as the general support assistant, and adjust later if needed
options.why: General-purpose guardrails are unlikely to meet specific regulatory requirements for financial decisions.

options.text: Add a generic disclaimer to every response
options.why: A disclaimer doesn't satisfy audit trail, sign-off or explainability requirements.

options.text: Ask legal to review after the feature is built
options.why: Legal review is necessary, but doing it only after building risks finding a blocking requirement too late.

bestCase.title: Rules mapped before a line of code
bestCase.example: The team identifies the specific disclosure, record-keeping and sign-off requirements for each region up front, designs the audit trail and approval threshold around them, and legal review confirms compliance before launch, not after.

worstCase.title: Rework after the fact
worstCase.example: The feature ships with the general assistant's guardrails. A compliance review three months in finds no audit trail exists for dispute decisions, and the feature is pulled while logging is retrofitted under a regulator's deadline.

steps.label: Identify the regulated scope
steps.goes: Payment disputes fall under financial regulation in each region.

steps.label: Map the specific requirements
steps.goes: Disclosure, record-keeping and sign-off rules are listed.
steps.goesWrong: The team skips this step and builds with the general assistant's guardrails instead.

steps.label: Design the audit trail
steps.goes: Every decision logs its inputs, reasoning summary and approver.

steps.label: Set a human sign-off threshold
steps.goes: Disputes above a set value require a qualified person's approval.

steps.label: Build explainability in
steps.goes: The system states which facts and rules led to each decision.

steps.label: Legal review before launch
steps.goes: Compliance confirms the design meets the mapped requirements.

takeaway: In regulated areas, map the specific rules first, then design audit trails, sign-off thresholds and explainability around them; don't retrofit compliance after building.
